newsitem.title: USA: US foreign crudes quiet ahead of stats, Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: US foreign crudes quiet ahead of stats, Iraq news.

text.p: Foreign crude trade on the U.S. Gulf Coast was subdued on Tuesday, as buyers and sellers waited for weekly inventory data and Iraqi news developments to provide market direction.
"People are just sitting back and trying to get a sense of where the market is," a Gulf Coast buyer said.
A Reuters forecast of forthcoming stock data from the American Petroleum Institute for the week ending July 4 shows a decline of one to two million barrels of gasoline.
Crude stocks were expected to drop by 2.5 million barrels, while refinery utilization was predicted to fall by 0.25 percent to 96.9 percent.
Crude imports were expected to extend their pattern of decline, reflecting the tight trans-Atlantic arbitrage.
The August spread between benchmarks West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and North Sea Brent was around $1.25-35 a barrel on Tuesday afternoon, down 10 cents from Monday afternoon.
Indeed, North Sea as well as West African offerings into the U.S. Gulf remain scarce, traders said.
Only a Norwegian company was offering one remaining cargo off a ULCC of Brent for August 15-20 delivery, asking around 25 cents under September WTI.
Norwegian Heidrun for mid-August delivery was also looking for a Gulf buyer at WTI minus $1.00 a barrel, traders said.
The dearth of trans-Atlantic pickings, coupled with declining freight rates, have lifted the price for Colombian Cusiana. Buyers are now asking about 75-80 cents under WTI.
The gasoline-rich grade was last done at WTI minus 90 cents a barrel.
Also out of Latin America, Argentine YPF was offering 950,000 barrels of Canadon Seco crude, loading around August 20-24, asking about $3.85 under WTI.
From Asia, a Swiss trading house was offering Indonesian Widuri, a high-pour-point grade, for July 17-21 arrival in the U.S. Gulf, asking WTI minus $1.30 a barrel, traders said.
Aside from the statistical data, traders were awaiting developments on the Iraqi front.
Iraq's ambassador to the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, told Reuters on Tuesday afternoon that U.N.-Iraqi talks on a key aid distribution plan are continuing.
It was not clear, however, whether agreement was near.

The aid plan must be hammered out before Iraq can resume oil exports under the U.N. oil-for-food accord, which allows Baghdad to sell $2.14 billion of oil over 180 days to buy and distribute humanitarian aid.
The second round of the program took effect on June 8, but exports have been stalled pending approval of the plan.
